I will also add this to the discussion. I have experience in building businesses from scratch.

You get a situation where a hobby starts out and grows, because the owner is good at the hobby - but they may not have a background in building a business - no real professional training - little understanding of the multitude of serious roadblocks that can mess things up.

What happens often is outside experienced business people come in with money and business expertise and buy into the situation - that means they also exert control and that often destroys the project - AKA DIGG.

Other times, the owners try to go on their own - and struggle along until they run into a serious roadblock - like a $6K bandwidth expense - and the project dies for lack of proper capitalization.

Many people question a guy like Alex Jones but completely fail to realize what it is he has actually achieved. He has managed to grow a tiny one man enterprise into a large and profitable growing concern, with studios and multiple full time employees, while still maintaining legal control of the business, and not substantially changing his core direction.

This would be the ideal outcome here as well. If the owner here would one day like to sell this operation for serious money, it must first demonstrate not only financial self sustainability - but also growth and profitability. This allows the owner to bring in outside investment money while still retaining controlling ownership of the business. AKA Facebook.

So you see - this whole issue of establishing some kind of management formality - even if the managers are volunteers for now - you do need to start setting up some formal organizational structure - because the work needed here has grown well beyond the abilities of any one man.

Businesses don't do this because they want to - they do it because they have to. The alternative is to pare the site back down to one that can be controlled and maintained by one man. Such a small operation is not really worth a whole lot financially... so it offers little for investors.

This is a decision that can only be made by the owners - everything depends on what the owners actually want to do - what is it exactly that they want to achieve - the vision of the future - That is legally the right of the owners to decide, and that decision belongs to nobody else.

If you decide to start taking risks with other peoples' money, there are legal requirements in how you structure your organization and how it operates - or you risk ALL of your personal assets. If you make a deal with some company, and you fuck up your end, even the volunteers can be held financially liable. If building companies is like getting married, closing them down is like getting divorced - it can be an extremely litigious and unpleasant experience. I've been there.

There is an army of talented people here - and this is indeed a powerful force - like any force it can do a lot of good, or a lot of harm, so I cannot stress enough the need for caution and careful reflection at precisely this moment in time. If you want to move forward on this, be damned sure you are fully committed. Because if we go it is probably going to be a wild ride:)
